Improving the energy performance of these buildings is essential to achieving energy affordability and improving grid resilience and has the potential to provide significant financial relief to U.S. households.1 Energy efficiency is a proven strategy that reduces building energy use and costs while optimizing the comfort and health of occupants. The energy efficiency sector is also a key economic driver across the nation, employing 2.3 million workers, a third of whom are in installation or repair occupations, and providing a median wage 20% higher than the U.S. median wage, with lower educational requirements to entry (DOE 2025). As the country accelerates efforts to modernize buildings and revitalize aging housing stock, the demand for skilled workers who can design, build, install, and operate high-performance, energy-efficient systems is growing rapidly, especially as older generations retire. However, the 2025 U.S. Energy and Employment Report found that at least 79% of employers across energy technologies report that it is “somewhat difficult or very difficult” to find qualified workers, with the most common reasons being a lack of experience, training, or technical skills, as well as insufficient nontechnical skills. Other reasons cited by employers include insufficient qualifications and small applicant pools (DOE 2025). As industry and governments nationwide confront persistent worker shortages and critical skill gaps, workforce development has emerged as a crucial strategy for cultivating needed talent— both by training new entrants and by upskilling existing employees. To support these efforts, research has explored ways to design effective training programs, examining which occupations face the greatest demand, the barriers to entering the energy efficiency sector, employers’ experiences in the labor market, and proven strategies for workforce development. Yet much of this work has not focused on understanding the motivations and decision-making practices of a key set of workforce stakeholders: building efficiency contractors. Contractors play a pivotal role in shaping the workforce through hiring, offering on-the-job learning opportunities, and defining training and credentials when engaged by workforce development practitioners. This report attempts to address this gap by investigating the motivations and risk perceptions of contractors when it comes to hiring and training employees to implement advanced building technologies. The report begins with an overview of the project’s methodology, then provides detailed information on the survey results. Finally, the conclusion offers key insights and takeaways. Gaining insight into these decision-making processes is vital for developing workforce programs that are responsive to contractors’ needs and effectively mitigate perceived risks.
